1002.title: Take off your shoes
1002.hook: at the burning bush, Moses is told the ground is holy (Exodus 3:1–5)
1002.howItsDone: Muslims remove their shoes before praying in a mosque, and shoes come off in Hindu and Sikh temples too; Jews and Christians read the burning bush in Exodus 3 as the moment Moses is called.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Solomon, the king a wildflower outdressed. Your line was dressed better than a king.

Moses isn't looking for anything. Exodus sets the scene plainly, in the King James words: "Now Moses kept the flock of Jethro his father in law, the priest of Midian: and he led the flock to the backside of the desert". A shepherd at work, far from anywhere, with someone else's sheep. Then, at the edge of his vision, a bush on fire. The fire isn't the strange part. The strange part is what it isn't doing.
screen: `A SHEPHERD AT WORK.` → `A BUSH ON FIRE.` → `WHAT IT ISN'T DOING.`

segments.voice: First, the sight. Exodus says "the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed." Fire that doesn't use anything up: a plain thing doing something it shouldn't. Second, the turn. Moses says: "I will now turn aside, and see this great sight, why the bush is not burnt." He leaves the path and stops herding long enough to look. The next line is the hinge of the story: "And when the LORD saw that he turned aside to see, God called unto him out of the midst of the bush". In the text, the call comes after the turning aside. Third, the instruction: "Draw not nigh hither: put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground." Notice where the holiness is. Not in a temple. Exodus calls this Horeb, the mountain of God, but Moses came there with sheep, not to worship: the dirt under his own feet, at his ordinary work. Fourth, the gesture. Taking off shoes is a way the body says: this place is different, and I'm not in charge here. In mosques, shoes come off before prayer, and the Qur'an tells the same story, with Moses told to take off his shoes in the holy valley. Some homes ask guests to leave their shoes at the door. The feet go bare, and the ground can be felt.
screen: `A FIRE THAT DOESN'T CONSUME.` · `HE TURNED ASIDE TO SEE.` · `UNDER HIS OWN FEET.` · `SHOES OFF, GROUND FELT.` · then, large: `HOLY GROUND.`

segments.voice: If you can, take off your shoes, and socks too if you like, and stand, or sit with bare feet on the floor. Feel what's under you, tile, carpet, wood, grass, and the weight moving through your heels and the balls of your feet: the ground you were already standing on. If you pray, let the standing be your prayer; if not, let it be your attention.
Horeb. The mountain of God where Moses was told to take off his shoes, because the ordinary ground under his feet was holy. Today's word.
Your line: holy ground. The call came after Moses turned aside to see. Day one thousand two, done.

1003.title: The still small voice
1003.hook: not in the wind, earthquake or fire, but a still small voice (1 Kings 19:11–12)
1003.howItsDone: Jews and Christians read Elijah's story in 1 Kings 19 as a teaching about how God speaks; some people take it as a reason to sit in silence and listen.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Horeb, where Moses took off his shoes. Your line was holy ground.

Elijah is done. In the book of Kings, Queen Jezebel has sworn to kill the prophet. He runs into the wilderness, sits under a juniper tree, and asks to die. An angel wakes him and feeds him, and he walks on until he reaches a mountain and goes into a cave. There a voice asks him a strange question: "What doest thou here, Elijah?" Then he's told to go out and stand on the mountain, because the LORD is about to pass by.
screen: `ELIJAH IS DONE.` → `A CAVE ON THE MOUNTAIN.` → `WHAT DOEST THOU HERE?`

segments.voice: First, the noise. In the King James words: "and, behold, the LORD passed by, and a great and strong wind rent the mountains, and brake in pieces the rocks before the LORD; but the LORD was not in the wind: and after the wind an earthquake; but the LORD was not in the earthquake". Then a fire, and again: not in the fire. Wind, earthquake, fire: the things that usually announce power. Each one arrives, and each one is empty. Second, the quiet: "and after the fire a still small voice." No thunder, no blaze. Some readers hear the Hebrew as something even quieter than a voice: a thin silence. Whatever it was, it was small. Third, Elijah's response. He's been through the wind and the earthquake, but it's the quiet that moves him. When Elijah heard it, the text says, he wrapped his face in his mantle and went out and stood at the mouth of the cave. Awe, here, comes in at a whisper. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary day. A lot of life is wind and earthquake and fire: notifications, headlines, arguments, alarms. The story suggests that what matters most may not be the loudest thing in the room. For Jews and Christians, this is about how God speaks. For anyone, it's an invitation to make enough quiet to hear something small.
screen: `NOT IN THE WIND, QUAKE OR FIRE.` · `A STILL SMALL VOICE.` · `HE WRAPPED HIS FACE.` · `NOT THE LOUDEST THING.` · then, large: `STILL SMALL VOICE.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes if you like, and notice the loud things first, traffic, voices in another room, your own busy thoughts, letting each one pass by like Elijah's wind. Then listen underneath for the quietest thing you can find: your breath, the hum of the room, the small silence between two sounds. If you pray, listen the way Elijah did, with nothing to say, and stay a minute past the bell if you'd like.
Elijah. The prophet who heard, after the wind, the earthquake and the fire, a quiet so small it moved him more than all the noise. Today's word.
Your line: still small voice. Wind, earthquake, fire, and then the quiet. That's day one thousand three.

chat.meaning: The LORD was not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire. After the fire came a still small voice, and Elijah wrapped his face in his mantle.

1004.title: Holy, holy, holy
1004.hook: Isaiah sees the seraphim calling: holy, holy, holy (Isaiah 6:1–3)
1004.carry: taken apart, then put back together
1004.howItsDone: Jews say the seraphim's words in the Kedushah, part of the repeated Amidah prayer, and Christians sing them in the Sanctus at the Eucharist; both come from Isaiah 6:3.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Elijah, who heard a still small voice after the fire. Your line was still small voice.

Isaiah dates his vision by a king's death. In the King James words: "In the year that king Uzziah died I saw also the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and his train filled the temple." A king has died, and in the temple Isaiah sees something that fills the room past its edges: the hem of a robe so vast it pours through the whole building. Above the throne stand the seraphim, calling one word to each other, three times over.
screen: `THE YEAR THE KING DIED.` → `HIS TRAIN FILLED THE TEMPLE.` → `THE SERAPHIM.`

segments.voice: First, the seraphim. The text describes them carefully: "each one had six wings; with twain he covered his face, and with twain he covered his feet, and with twain he did fly." Even these beings cover their faces. Awe, in Isaiah, isn't staring. It's knowing you can't quite look. Second, the call: "And one cried unto another, and said, Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts". Three times, back and forth, as if once couldn't hold it. In Hebrew the word is qadosh. Jewish prayer takes up these words in the Kedushah, and Christian worship sings them in the Sanctus. Third, the half of the line that's easy to miss: "the whole earth is full of his glory." The holiness isn't kept inside the temple. It spills out to the edges of the world, so the street outside, the market, the field, a kitchen, could all be places where that glory sits. Fourth, the human answer. Isaiah doesn't say how wonderful. He says: "Woe is me! for I am undone". Undone: in the old English sense, ruined, come apart. In the story, one of the seraphim flies to him with a live coal from the altar, touches his lips, and his sin is purged. Awe takes him apart before it puts him back together. And the seraphim's line leaves a question: what would it be like to call one ordinary thing holy, and mean it?
screen: `EVEN THE SERAPHIM COVER THEIR FACES.` · `HOLY, HOLY, HOLY.` · `THE WHOLE EARTH IS FULL.` · `WOE IS ME: UNDONE.` · then, large: `HOLY.`

segments.voice: Choose one ordinary thing in reach, a cup, a key, your own hand, and rest your eyes on it: where it came from, who made it, what it has held. Then say one word over it, quietly or inside: holy, not because it's special, but because the seraphim said the whole earth is full. If you pray, you can say their words themselves; if the word feels too big, just look a little longer.
Holy. In Hebrew, qadosh: the word the seraphim call to each other three times in Isaiah's vision, with the whole earth full of glory. Today's word.
Your line: taken apart, then put back together. Woe is me came first; the live coal came after. See you tomorrow.

1005.title: I knew it not
1005.hook: Jacob wakes: surely the Lord is in this place, and I knew it not (Genesis 28:16)
1005.howItsDone: Jews and Christians read Jacob's dream at Bethel in Genesis 28 as a story of God meeting a person in an unexpected place; some people repeat Jacob's words when they notice an ordinary place anew.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was holy, the seraphim's word, called three times. Your line was taken apart, then put back together.

A man on the run, alone, with the brother he cheated behind him. That's Jacob in Genesis, long before the day Esau runs to meet him. The sun goes down on him in the middle of nowhere. The King James text is almost offhand: "he lighted upon a certain place, and tarried there all night, because the sun was set". No shrine, nothing to mark it. He takes a stone for a pillow and lies down on the ground. A certain place. Any place.
screen: `JACOB ON THE RUN.` → `A CERTAIN PLACE.` → `A STONE FOR A PILLOW.`

segments.voice: First, the dream: "and behold a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven: and behold the angels of God ascending and descending on it." Notice where the ladder stands: on the earth, right where a tired man is sleeping on a rock. In the dream, heaven isn't somewhere else; it touches down here. Second, the waking: "And Jacob awaked out of his sleep, and he said, Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not." The place didn't change overnight. Jacob did. In his own words, the LORD was in this place when he arrived, when he chose the stone, while he slept. He just didn't know. Third, the fear: "And he was afraid, and said, How dreadful is this place! this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven." Dreadful sounds strange to a modern ear. Here it sits close to awe, the trembling side from the start of this block. Fourth, the new name. Jacob sets up his stone as a pillar and calls the place Bethel. Genesis adds that the city had been called Luz before. The same ground, two names: one from before he knew, one from after. For Jews and Christians, Bethel is a place where God met Jacob. For anyone, it raises a quiet question: how many certain places, ordinary as a roadside, do people pass through without knowing?
screen: `A LADDER SET UP ON THE EARTH.` · `THE PLACE DIDN'T CHANGE. JACOB DID.` · `HOW DREADFUL IS THIS PLACE.` · `LUZ BECOMES BETHEL.` · then, large: `AND I KNEW IT NOT.`

segments.voice: Stay exactly where you are, and look at this place as if you'd just woken up in it after a long journey: the corners, the light, the sounds, what you've stopped seeing because it's always here. Then, if it feels right, say Jacob's words quietly: and I knew it not. If you pray, you can say the whole line; if not, the looking is enough.
Bethel. The place Jacob named on waking, where in his telling the LORD had been there all along, and he was the one who changed. Today's word.
Your line: and I knew it not. Luz before, Bethel after: the same ground, two names. Day one thousand five.

screen: `DAY 1005 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SIGNS FOR THOSE WHO THINK.`

1006.title: Signs for those who think
1006.hook: in the heavens and earth and the turning of night and day are signs (Quran 3:190)
1006.howItsDone: Muslims recite the closing verses of Surah Al Imran, and some recite them on waking in the night, following the report that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ did; reflection on creation is called tafakkur.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Bethel, where Jacob woke and said, I knew it not. Your line was and I knew it not.

Late at night, a man gets up from his bed and looks at the sky. A report in the hadith collection of al-Bukhari tells it this way: Ibn Abbas was staying in the house, and saw the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, wake in the night, look up at the heavens, and recite the closing verses of the Qur'an's third chapter. Those verses begin with the sky, and with the plain fact that night turns into day. Here, awe and thinking go together.
screen: `AWAKE IN THE NIGHT.` → `LOOKING AT THE HEAVENS.` → `A SCRIPTURE THAT SAYS: THINK.`

segments.voice: First, the verse. In paraphrase, Surah Al Imran says: in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and in the alternation of night and day, there are signs for people of understanding. Nothing exotic: sky, ground, and the fact that it gets dark and then light again. Second, the word signs. In Arabic it's ayat. A sign points past itself, the way a road sign isn't the city but tells you the city is there. In Islamic teaching the world is full of these pointers, and Muslims use the same word, ayat, for the Qur'an's own verses. The book has signs, and so does the sky. Third, who sees them. The verse doesn't say signs for everyone. It says signs for people of understanding. The next verse describes them: people who remember God standing, sitting and lying down, who reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth, and say: our Lord, you did not create this in vain. Remembering and thinking, together. Awe, here, isn't the end of thought. It's where thought goes when it follows something all the way. Fourth, what it asks of an ordinary day. The turning of night and day happens whether anyone notices or not. The verse asks for noticing, and then for a question: what is this pointing to? For Muslims, the answer is God. For anyone, the turning of the day is still there to watch, and to think about.
screen: `HEAVENS, EARTH, NIGHT AND DAY.` · `AYAT: SIGNS THAT POINT PAST.` · `FOR PEOPLE WHO THINK.` · `NOTICE, THEN ASK.` · then, large: `SIGNS.`

segments.voice: Find the light where you are, a window, a doorway, the way it falls across the room, and tell the time of day by the light alone: high and white, low and gold, gray, or electric, and which way the shadows lean. Then ask one quiet question, and don't rush it: what is this pointing to? If you pray, you can remember God as you sit, as the verse describes; if not, let the question stay open.
Ayat. The Qur'an's word for signs, pointing past themselves in the sky, the earth and the turning of night and day, for people who reflect. Today's word.
Your line: signs. Sky, ground and the turning of the day, for people who think. Day one thousand six, done.

1007.title: Light upon light
1007.hook: the Verse of Light: God is the light of the heavens and earth, a lamp in a niche
1007.carry: almost glowing before the fire arrives
1007.howItsDone: Muslims recite the Verse of Light (Quran 24:35) in prayer and study, and commentators and Sufi writers have reflected on what the niche, the glass, the lamp and the oil might stand for.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was ayat, signs for people who think. Your line was signs.

A small hollow set into a wall. Inside it, a lamp. Around the flame, a glass so clear it shines like a star. The oil comes from an olive tree, and it would almost glow on its own, even if no fire touched it. That's the whole scene: a lamp in a niche. It sounds like a room in an old house at night. But it's in the Quran, the likeness it gives for God's light, and it's known as the Verse of Light.
screen: `A LAMP IN A NICHE.` → `A GLASS LIKE A STAR.` → `THE VERSE OF LIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, the size of it. The verse opens as big as a sentence can get. In Pickthall's translation: "Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth." Not a light in the sky. The light of all of it. Second, the shrinking. Right after that huge opening, the verse gives a likeness, a picture, and the picture is tiny: a niche, a lamp, a glass, an olive tree. The tree, it adds, is neither of the east nor of the west; it belongs to no one direction. So the light that fills everything is shown at the size of something you could hold in your two hands. Third, the layers. The niche holds the lamp. The glass makes the flame shine like a star. The oil is already almost glowing before the fire arrives. Each piece adds to the brightness. Then the verse sums it up in three words: "Light upon light." Fourth, who sees it. The verse goes on to say that God guides to His light whom He will, and that God speaks to people in likenesses. Readers have heard the layers in different ways. Some see the niche as the human heart, and the lamp as what shines inside it. Others keep it as a picture of God that no explanation fully opens. The verse itself doesn't decode the picture. It hands you the lamp and lets you look.
screen: `THE LIGHT OF THE HEAVENS AND THE EARTH.` · `SHOWN AT THE SIZE OF A LAMP.` · `NICHE, GLASS, FLAME, OIL.` · `A LIKENESS, NOT A MAP.` · then, large: `LIGHT UPON LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Light one candle, or switch on one lamp and turn the others off, or find the brightest small thing in the room, even a patch of daylight on the wall. Let your eyes rest on the layers: the flame or the bulb, the glow around it, the light it throws on things nearby. If you pray, you can hold the verse's opening words; if not, just watch the light do what it does.
Niche. The small hollow holding the lamp in the Quran's Verse of Light, a picture of the light of the heavens and the earth. Today's word.
Your line: almost glowing before the fire arrives. Niche, glass, flame and oil: light upon light. See you tomorrow.

1008.title: Wherever you turn
1008.hook: to God belong east and west; wherever you turn, there is God's face
1008.howItsDone: Muslims pray facing the Kaaba in Mecca, and recite verses such as Quran 2:115 to remember that God is not confined to any one direction or place.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was niche, where the lamp sits in the Verse of Light. Your line was almost glowing before the fire arrives. This week: holy ground, a still small voice, holy, holy, holy, Jacob waking, and signs.

Which way does a room face? A classroom faces the board. A theater faces the stage. A couch, somehow, faces the TV. People arrange themselves around a front without thinking about it, and when something matters, they turn toward it. Now take that habit to the biggest scale there is. If you wanted to face God, which way would you turn? One short verse in the Quran answers that question, and its answer isn't a direction on a compass.
screen: `WHICH WAY DOES A ROOM FACE?` → `WE TURN TOWARD WHAT MATTERS.` → `WHICH WAY IS GOD?`

segments.voice: First, the directions themselves. The verse, in Pickthall's translation, begins: "Unto Allah belong the East and the West". East is where the day starts; west is where it ends. Both belong to God. No side of the map is left out. Second, the turn: "and whithersoever ye turn, there is Allah's Countenance." Whithersoever is an old word for wherever. Turn left, turn right, turn all the way around: the verse names no place where the turning works and no place where it doesn't. Third, the face. Countenance is Pickthall's word for the Arabic wajh, which means face. A face is not just a surface. It's where someone is present to you, where they're looking back. So some readers hear more here than God being everywhere, like air. They hear a face in every direction, a presence turned toward them. Fourth, how this sits with prayer. Muslims pray facing the Kaaba in Mecca, and a little later in the same chapter the Quran speaks of that direction for prayer. The two sit side by side in one chapter. Prayer has a direction, and the community faces it together. And this verse sets no limit on where God's face is. Some readers put it this way: one is about how people gather, the other about where God can be found. The verse ends by calling God All-Embracing. In the verse's picture, no turn steps outside it.
screen: `THE EAST AND THE WEST BELONG TO GOD.` · `WHEREVER YE TURN.` · `WAJH: A FACE TURNED TOWARD YOU.` · `A DIRECTION FOR PRAYER, A FACE EVERYWHERE.` · then, large: `THERE IS ALLAH'S COUNTENANCE.`

segments.voice: Stand if you can, or turn your head and shoulders if you're sitting, and face one way for a breath, noticing what's there: a wall, a window, a door. Then turn a little and breathe again, and keep going slowly until you've come all the way around, holding the verse lightly: wherever you turn. If you pray, let each turn be a small greeting; if not, let each direction count as much as the last.
Wajh. The Arabic word for face, behind the Quran's countenance: wherever you turn, there is God's face. Today's word.
Your line: no turn steps outside it. East, west, and every direction in between. A week of awe, complete.
